title: Knowledge of others' minds (3.19)
hook: samyama on another person's state of mind reveals that mind, and the very next sutra draws a line around what it can't see

segments.voice: Yesterday: siddhi, and the powers begin. See how a thing changes, all the way, and time opens in both directions.

Your phone buzzes. It's your oldest friend. One word: hey. No punctuation. And somehow you already know something's wrong. Not what. Just that. You've read a thousand of their heys, and this one is different. Nobody calls that a superpower. It's what close attention to one person, for years, starts to do. Patanjali names a power that sounds like a much bigger version of that. And then, immediately, he tells you exactly where it stops.
screen: `ONE WORD: HEY.` → `SOMETHING'S WRONG.` → `NOT WHAT. JUST THAT.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.19: by samyama on the idea in another's mind, knowledge of that other mind. The word is pratyaya, the content of awareness at a given moment, the mood or idea running through it. Rest concentration, meditation and absorption on that, and the other person's state of mind becomes clear: troubled, calm, grasping, glad. Then comes the warning, in the very next line. Sutra 3.20: but not its object. You can know that the mind is angry, but not what it's angry at, because that wasn't the object of the samyama. The classical commentary is careful here. The power reaches the color of the mind, not its whole story. Even at its height, knowing another person has a limit, and the sutra writes the limit right into the power. Notice the order of the book, too. Patanjali didn't open with powers. He opened with non-harm, truth, not stealing. Anyone who reads a mind is standing very close to someone else's inner life, and the first limb has already said how to stand there. Now the week, from the top. Pranayama, the veil thins. Pratyahara, the senses follow the mind home. Concentration, meditation, absorption. Prajna, samyama. The transformations, what changes. Past and future. And today, other minds, with a line drawn around them. A week that went inward, and now begins to turn outward again, toward what that inward work can do.
screen: `PRATYAYA: WHAT'S IN A MIND NOW.` · `KNOW THE MIND, NOT ITS OBJECT.` · `THE LIMIT IS WRITTEN IN.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `AND THE WARNING.`

segments.voice: Ask what color your own mind is right now, restless, tired, glad, worried, and name it in one word without chasing the reasons. Breathe with it. Then, if you like, bring to mind someone you love and wish their mind well, whatever color it is today.
Pratyaya, the mood or idea running through someone's awareness. By samyama on another's state of mind, that mind is known, though not what it's fixed on.
Your line: and the warning. The mood can be known; the reason stays theirs. A week of inner limbs, done.

howItsDone: Many Hindu stories describe sages who know the minds of those who come to them, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras point to 3.20's limit and to the yamas as the frame in which any such power is held.

original.note: Sanskrit para-citta-jñāna: knowledge (jñāna) of another's (para) mind (citta), 3.19.

trapdoor: what you thought: yogis claim to read minds.
what it means: samyama on another's state of mind reveals that state, but not what the mind is fixed on.
what a scholar hears: pratyayasya para-citta-jnanam (3.19); na ca tat salambanam (3.20), the support or object not included; numbering of these sutras varies by edition.

chat.says: If a yogi could read minds, would they know exactly what you're upset about?
options: No, 3.20 says the power knows the mind's state, not what it's fixed on.
Yes, every thought and its reason would be open to them like a book.
Only if they had also known you personally for many years beforehand.
chat.meaning: Sutra 3.19 gives knowledge of another's state of mind; 3.20 adds, but not its object. The limit is written into the power.

pratyaya.meaning: the mood or idea in a mind at a given moment

Pratyahara.meaning: drawing back the senses, the fifth limb of yoga

samyama.meaning: concentration, meditation and absorption held on one object
